title: Sorting algorithms
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 7
subtitle: Eight ways to put numbers in order — and why “how many comparisons” is the question.

sections.title: What to ask of a sort
sections.body: Sorting puts records in order by a key. Properties: internal (fits in memory) versus external (merges from disk); stable (equal keys keep their relative order — important when sorting by one column after another); in place (O(1) extra memory); adaptive (faster on nearly-sorted input). Compare with the same seven numbers 5 1 4 2 8 9 3 in the figures below.

choices.text: Keeps equal keys in their original relative order.
Always runs in O(n log n).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sort names by city, then by surname: a stable second pass keeps city order within equal surnames.

sections.title: Bubble, selection, insertion
sections.body: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; the largest value “bubbles” to the end each pass (20 comparisons, 8 swaps here). Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into place: always n(n−1)/2 comparisons (21) but at most n−1 swaps. Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix, inserting each new item by shifting larger ones right: great on nearly sorted data (best case O(n)).

questions.prompt: Which simple sort is best on an almost-sorted array?

choices.text: Insertion sort — few shifts are needed.

sections.title: Quick sort and merge sort
sections.body: Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges: always O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space (12 comparisons here). Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions smaller-left/larger-right, and recurses: O(n log n) on average, in place, but O(n²) in the worst case (already sorted input with a bad pivot rule) (13 comparisons).

worked.why: Why O(n log n)? Halving gives log₂n levels and each level does O(n) merging work.
For n = 1024 that is about 10 levels × 1024 ≈ 10 240 operations, versus 1 048 576 for n².

questions.prompt: When does quick sort degrade to O(n²)?

choices.text: When partitions are badly unbalanced, e.g. always picking the smallest or largest element as pivot.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One side gets n−1 elements every time.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Random input is its average case.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Size alone does not cause it.

sections.title: Heap sort and Shell sort
sections.body: Heap sort builds a max-heap then repeatedly swaps the root (largest) to the end and sifts down: O(n log n) worst case, in place, not stable (19 comparisons here). Shell sort runs insertion sort on elements far apart first (gap sequence n/2, n/4, …, 1) so elements move long distances early: no simple tight bound but far better than plain insertion in practice.

questions.prompt: Heap sort’s main advantage over merge sort?

choices.text: It sorts in place with guaranteed O(n log n).
It is faster on sorted input.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Merge sort needs O(n) extra space.

sections.title: Radix sort: no comparisons
sections.body: Any sort that compares keys needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Radix sort avoids comparing: it distributes numbers into ten buckets by the least significant digit, collects them in order (stably), then repeats for the next digit. With d digits it costs O(d·n). 170 45 75 90 802 24 2 66 becomes 2 24 45 66 75 90 170 802.

questions.prompt: Why must each radix pass be stable?

choices.text: So the order from earlier (less significant) digits survives within each later bucket.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Otherwise earlier work would be undone.

problems.prompt: Sort 5 1 4 2 8 9 3 with each algorithm and compare the comparison counts.
problems.answer: Bubble 20, selection 21, insertion 13, shell 14, quick 13, merge 12, heap 19. The quadratic sorts do visibly more work, and the gap widens quickly with n.
